headline: Earlier today, the Iraqi Armed Forces shot down an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in the Muwailihah area, north of Babylon Governorate, southern Iraq. There is considerable speculation regarding the UAV's identity, with some suggesting it could be a Chinese-made CH-4B or Wing Loong II operated by the Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF). However, the wreckage appears to show a 4-blade composite pusher propeller, whereas both the CH-4B and Wing Loong II are equipped with 3-blade pusher propellers. Based on that detail, those two platforms seem unlikely. The only UAVs that come to mind with a 4-blade pusher propeller are the MQ-9B (SkyGuardian/SeaGuardian) and the MQ-9A Extended Range (ER). The standard MQ-9A (Block 1/Block 5) uses a 3-blade propeller.

headline: If that didn't happen in the last war, when Iran was launching an average of 40 ballistic missiles per day for weeks, how do you expect to do it now, especially after massively depleting your JASSM stockpile? People need to stay grounded in reality. There's a reason Trump ended the campaign two days ago instead of continuing it: it simply wasn't sustainable. You can't keep pounding Iran indefinitely while seeing no meaningful results. Iran isn't winning or losing. It's simply forcing the United States to burn through its munitions. The targeted bases are still operational, damaged entrances can be repaired within hours, and after 40 days of fighting, they destroyed only around three launchers (documented). Iranian launchers are also relatively easy to build since they rely on hydraulic systems. On top of that, no actual evidence has been presented showing that Iran's ballistic missile production was significantly degraded. In fact, both Iranian officials and U.S. media have since reported that production not only continues but has accelerated since the war. Meanwhile, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the United States expended between 3,710 and 4,510 key precision-guided munitions during the Iran War, equivalent to roughly 31–38% of its estimated pre-war stockpile. Air defense interceptors saw the steepest depletion, with an estimated 190–290 of 360 THAAD interceptors expended (up to 80%), 130–250 of 410 SM-3 interceptors (more than half), and 1,060–1,430 of 2,330 Patriot interceptors (up to 61%). Long-range strike weapons were also heavily consumed. The analysis estimates the U.S. fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 1,100 JASSM air-launched cruise missiles, and 40–70 of its estimated 90 Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs), leaving the relatively new missile with a significantly reduced inventory. Replenishing some of the most heavily used weapons could take years. No matter how much damage is inflicted on Iranian infrastructure, whether civilian or military, repairs are relatively quick and inexpensive. If this continues, the situation could eventually shift, because the day Iran fields a capable air force, the United States and Israel won't be able to operate as freely as they do today. During the last conflict, IRGC Aerospace Force missile units had enough freedom of action to carry out what was effectively a counter-force campaign against high-value U.S. targets at ranges exceeding 1,000 km.

According to the Journal, Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine warned the White House that declining inventories of Patriot and other interceptors would increase the risk to U.S. forces if large scale operations resumed. The report also says the White House sought to prevent publication of updated government figures on Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Air Defense (THAAD) interceptor expenditures, arguing their release could harm national security. President Donald J. Trump disputed reports of a munitions shortfall, telling the Journal the U.S. has "far more munitions than we need." Outside analysts, however, have warned that the high rate of interceptor use in the conflict could strain U.S. air defense capacity and affect readiness for other potential contingencies. headline: Axios reports that U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Adm. Brad Cooper recommended ending the recent bombing campaign around the Strait of Hormuz after concluding it had largely achieved its objectives and reached the limit of its effectiveness. According to Axios, Cooper told senior defense officials that two weeks of strikes had significantly degraded Iran's ability to attack shipping and that most planned targets had already been hit. He reportedly said the remaining roughly 20% of designated Operation Epic Fury targets would require a return to major combat operations, and that absent such a decision, there was little military value in continuing the limited bombing campaign. Axios says Cooper's assessment, along with warnings from Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine about dwindling air defense interceptor stocks, helped influence President Trump's decision to pause U.S. strikes on Friday. The report adds that U.S.-Iran talks are continuing while both sides appear to be observing an informal "quiet for quiet" pause.

headline: According to TankerTrackers, the merchant vessel identified by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) as the Mozambique-flagged M/T Lavine is the same ship operating under the name M/T Disha (IMO 8818219). CENTCOM says the vessel repeatedly attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iran, ignored multiple warnings, and was ultimately disabled after U.S. forces fired into its engine room on July 24th. TankerTrackers reports it first observed the vessel entering the U.S. blockade perimeter on July 23. The organization notes the tanker has been under U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions for the past two years and alleges it previously transported Iranian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to the Houthis in Yemen. The Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) says the vessel was carrying 28 Indian seafarers, all of whom survived the incident. The union alleges the strike targeted the vessel's accommodation area. However, video shared by the organization appears to show flames emanating from a hatch at the base of the smokestack, directly above the engine room, which is broadly consistent with CENTCOM's statement that U.S. forces disabled the vessel by firing into its engine room. The footage alone does not conclusively establish the exact point of impact. Source: https://x.com/FSUIINDIA/status/2080892015332749709?s=20

headline: Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on China: China is an important neighboring country. Since I became Prime Minister, my policy has consistently been to comprehensively promote our strategic mutually beneficial relationship with China and to build a constructive and stable bilateral relationship. Precisely because there are concerns and challenges between Japan and China, it is essential that we engage in dialogue at every level and on every possible occasion to deepen mutual understanding. We will continue communicating closely with the Chinese side while responding calmly and appropriately from the standpoint of Japan's national interests.

headline: Zelensky : "I had a big problem, not for days or weeks, but for months, in the work and dialogue between the Chief of the Army and the Ministry of Defense. There are some things we have to manage, and you can manage them only if the ministry works with the army. You can't manage it one side or another." "The big challenge is mobilization. We may face 500,000 more Russian troops. We need a new attitude to mobilization and new steps. I need unanimity between these two institutions." "The second point is air defense. We don't have enough anti-ballistic systems. I don't have time for talks. I don't have time to listen to one side, then listen to another side, because the two sides are not ready to meet every day, they have to meet every hour until our sky is protected." "I don't need to find who is right and who is not right."
